Latvian Gas & Water Utilities Disrupted Amid Political Unrest as Protesters Blockade Key Sites

RIGA — Operations across Latvia’s gas and water utilities sector have been thrown into turmoil after coordinated protest action blocked access to several major facilities on Wednesday. Protesters, who authorities say are part of a political movement objecting to recent government policy changes, have occupied or blockaded multiple sites in Riga and across the Kurzeme region, affecting both gas distribution and water treatment plants. The most significant disruption is reported at the Inčukalns underground gas storage facility, a critical node in Latvia’s energy infrastructure.

Latvijas Gaze, the country’s largest natural gas provider, confirmed Wednesday afternoon that access to its Riga control center and several regional stations had been obstructed. “Due to the ongoing blockade, we are unable to guarantee the continuity of regular operations,” said Inese Ozola, spokesperson for Latvijas Gaze. “Our priority is ensuring public safety and the integrity of the infrastructure, but the situation remains highly volatile.”

The Latvian Utilities Association reported that two water treatment plants in Liepāja and Ventspils, operated by Daugava Utilities Group, have also been affected. “The blockades have forced staff to remain inside for extended periods, and deliveries of critical chemicals are currently suspended,” said association chair Juris Kalniņš. “We are working closely with authorities to secure access and to prevent any risk of service interruption.”

While there have been no immediate reports of widespread outages, both industry officials and analysts warn that prolonged disruption could have serious consequences. “If these blockades persist beyond 48 hours, we could see localized reductions in water pressure and possible interruptions to gas supply, particularly in outlying areas,” said Māris Petersons, senior energy analyst at Baltic Policy Institute. “Latvia’s energy storage facilities are robust, but they are not designed to operate indefinitely without on-site management.”

The Ministry of Economics has called for calm and urged dialogue between protesters and utility operators. “We are monitoring the situation closely and are prepared to facilitate negotiations,” said Minister Līga Rudzīte in a statement. “The uninterrupted operation of gas and water utilities is essential for public welfare, and we appeal for the immediate cessation of all blockades.”

The Latvian Gas & Water Workers’ Union expressed concern for the safety of staff and called for swift action to resolve the dispute. “Our members are dedicated to maintaining essential services, but their well-being must not be put at risk,” said union leader Artūrs Bērziņš. 

As of late Wednesday, the occupation and blockades remained in place, with no clear resolution in sight. Industry observers anticipate that the coming hours will be crucial for determining whether the disruption will escalate into a full-scale supply crisis.
